translations.text: The Saviour Christ, after he came into this life and had grown to be a man, when he was thirty years old in his human nature, then began to work miracles, and chose the twelve disciples, whom we call apostles.
Then they were with him ever afterwards, and he taught them all the wisdom that stands in holy books, and through them established all Christendom.
Then they said to the Saviour, "Lord, teach us how we may pray." Then the Saviour answered, and said this:
"Pray with these words to my Father and to your Father, God Almighty: Pater noster, which is in English, You, our Father, who are in heaven, may your name be hallowed.
May your kingdom come. May your will be done on earth just as in heaven. Give us today our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. So be it."
God the Father Almighty has one Son by nature and many by adoption. Christ is God's Son in such a way that the Father begot him of himself, without any mother.
The Father has no body, nor did he beget his Child in the way that men do:
but his Wisdom, with which he made all creatures, is his Son, who is eternally from the Father and with the Father, God from God, just as mighty as the Father.
We men are God's children, because he made us; and afterwards, when we were ruined by sin, he sent his own Child for our redemption.
Now we are God's children, and Christ is our brother, if we rightly obey the Father and honour him with all our mind.
Christ is our head, and we are his limbs: he is clothed with our human nature, and he has our body, which he took from the holy virgin Mary;
Therefore we may call to him with confidence, as to our brother, if we keep the brotherhood as he taught us;
that is, that we must not allow the devil to entice us away from Christ's brotherhood by any vices.
Truly, the man who imitates the devil is the devil's child, not by nature or by creation, but through that imitation and his evil deeds.
And the person who pleases God is God's child, not by nature, but by creation and by good merits, just as Christ said in his gospel,
"Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and my mother, and my sister."
Therefore now all Christian people, both powerful and lowly, both nobly born and not nobly born, both the lord and the servant, are all brothers, and all have one Father in heaven.
The wealthy man is no better in this name than the poor man. The servant may call on God as his Father just as boldly as the king.
We are all equal before God, unless one surpasses another in good works. The rich man must not despise the poor man because of his wealth, for the poor man is often better before God than the rich.
God is our Father, therefore we must all be brothers in God, and keep the brotherly bond unbroken;
that is, true peace, so that each of us loves the other as himself, and commands nothing of anyone that he would not want to be commanded of him.
He who keeps this is God's child, and Christ and all the holy people who thrive in God are his brothers and his sisters.
We say, "Pater noster qui es in celis," that is, "Our Father who are in heaven," because God the Father is in heaven, and he is everywhere, just as he himself said,
"I fill heaven and earth with myself." And again the holy gospel says this about him:
"Heaven is his throne, and earth is his footstool." We turn eastward when we pray, because the heaven rises from there:
not as if his dwelling were in the east alone, and he abandoned the west or other regions, he who is present everywhere, not through the extent of space, but through the presence of his majesty.

When we turn our face to the east, where the heaven rises, which surpasses all bodily things, then our mind should be reminded by this that it should be turned to the highest and foremost nature, that is, God.
We must also know that the sinful man is called earth and the righteous man is called heaven, because God dwells in righteous men, and the good man is the temple of the Holy Spirit.

So too, on the other hand, the wicked man is the devil's temple and the devil's dwelling. Therefore the difference between good men and evil men is as great as the difference between heaven and earth.
There are seven petitions in the Pater noster. In the first two words there are no petitions, but they are praises: that is,
"Our Father who are in heaven." The first petition is, "Sanctificetur nomen tuum," that is, "May your name be hallowed."
This is not to be understood as if God's name were not holy enough, for it was always holy and always will be, and he blesses and hallows us all.

Rather, this phrase is to be understood to mean that his name should be hallowed in us, and that he should grant us that we may bless his name with our mouths, and that he should give us the understanding to know that nothing is as holy as his name.
The second petition is, "Adveniat regnum tuum," that is, in our language, "May your kingdom come."

God's kingdom always was, and always will be; but it is to be understood in this way: that his kingdom may be over us, and that he may reign in us, and that we may be subject to him with all obedience,
and that our kingdom may be granted and fulfilled for us, just as Christ promised us that he would give us an eternal kingdom, saying this:
"Come, you blessed of my Father, and take possession of the kingdom that was prepared for you from the beginning of the world."
This will be our kingdom, if we earn it now; and we will be God's kingdom when Christ hands us over to his Father on Judgement Day, just as the holy scripture says,
"Cum tradiderit regnum Patri suo," that is, "When he hands over the kingdom to his Father."
What is the kingdom that he delivers to his Father, if not the holy people, both men and women, whom he redeemed from the torment of hell by his own death?
He will deliver them to his own Father at the end of this world. They will then be God's kingdom and will reign with God in eternity, both in soul and in body, and they will then be like the angels.
The third petition is "Fiat voluntas tua sicut in caelo et in terra," that is, "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven."
That is: just as the angels in heaven obey you and join themselves to you in every way, so also the people who are on earth [?]
and, made of earth, may they be obedient to your will, and join themselves to you with all eagerness.
Truly, God's will is done in those people who act according to God's will. Our soul is heavenly, and our body is earthly.

So with these words we also pray that God's will be done both in our soul and in our body, that both may obey him, and that he may keep and shield both our soul and our body from the devil's temptations.
The fourth petition is "Panem nostrum cotidianum da nobis hodie," that is, in our language, "Give us this day our daily bread."
This is to be understood in three senses: that he should give food to our body, and also give our soul the spiritual bread.

The spiritual bread is God's commandment, which we must think on every day and carry out in deeds. For just as the body lives on bodily food, so must the soul live on God's teaching and on spiritual meditations.

The body quickly wastes away and decays if its food is withheld from it. So too the soul perishes if it does not have the spiritual food, that is, God's commandments, by which it must thrive and be enriched.

The spiritual bread is also the holy housel [the Eucharist], with which we strengthen our faith. Through receiving the holy housel our sins are forgiven us, and we are strengthened against the devil's temptation.
Therefore we must often cleanse and strengthen our souls with that spiritual meal.
Yet whoever is ruined by grievous sins must not presume to receive God's housel unless he has first made amends for his sins. If he does otherwise, he receives it to his own harm.
The bread signifies three things, as we said. One is the body's food; the second is the soul's; the third is the receiving of the holy housel.
We must pray to our Lord every day for these three things.
The fifth petition is, "Et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris," that is,
"Forgive us our sins, just as we forgive those people who sin against us." We must do just as we promise in these words;
that is, that we be merciful among ourselves and, for the great love of God, forgive those people who sin against us, so that God Almighty may forgive us our sins.
But if we will not forgive the small offences of the people who have angered us, then God will not forgive us our great and many sins either, just as Christ himself said,
"When you stand at your prayers, forgive whatever you hold in your mind against anyone, and your Father, who is in heaven, will forgive you your sins.
If, then, you will not forgive from your inmost heart those who anger you, then your Father who is in heaven will not forgive you your sins either;

but he will command you to be bound and put in prison, that is, in the torment of hell; and there the devil will torture you until you have suffered for all your offences, until you come to the last farthing."
It is, however, taught according to God's ordinance that wise men must correct foolish men, so that they put aside their folly and their vices, and yet must love that man as their own brother.
The sixth petition is, "Et ne nos inducas in temptationem": that is, "Do not allow, O God, that we be led into temptation."
Temptation is one thing and testing is another. God tempts no one; and yet no one comes to God's kingdom unless he has been tested.
Therefore we should not pray that God not test us, but we should pray that God shield us, so that we do not fail in the testing.
The devil is allowed to test every person, to show whether he is worth anything or nothing, and whether he loves God with a sincere heart or goes about in hypocrisy;
As gold is tested in fire, so God tests a man's mind in various temptations, to see whether he is steadfast. God knows well enough how things will turn out in the temptation;
but a person has no great merit unless he has been tested. Through testing he will thrive, if he withstands the temptations.
If he falls, let him rise again: that is, if he sins, let him eagerly make amends for it and afterwards stop; for no amends are worth anything unless there is stopping.
The person who sins often and makes amends often angers God; and the more he sins, the more he is in the devil's power.
and then God abandons him, and he goes wherever the devil guides him, like a broken ship at sea, which goes wherever the wind drives it.
The more a good person is tested, the more cheerful he is and the nearer to God, until he passes with full merit from this life to the eternal life.

And the more often the evil man falls when he is tempted, the more wicked he becomes, and the nearer to the devil, until he passes from this life to the eternal torment, if he would not stop earlier, when he could and was allowed to.
For this reason God often waits for the evil man and gives him time, so that he may stop his wicked deeds and turn his mind to God before his end, if he will.
If he will not, then he is thrown into the devil's hands with every justice, without any excuse.

Therefore it is better now for Christians to earn, through hardships and toil, the eternal kingdom and the eternal bliss with God and all his saints, than to earn, through ease and evil desires, the eternal torments with all the devils in the punishment of hell.
The seventh petition is "Sed libera nos a malo," that is, "But deliver us from evil": deliver us from the devil and from all his snares. God loves us, and the devil hates us.
God feeds us and comforts us, and the devil wants to kill us, if he is allowed to. But he is prevented by God's protection, as long as we do not want to destroy ourselves with vices.
Therefore we must shun and despise the wicked devil with all his tricks, because he has no claim on us, and we must love and follow our Lord, who leads us to eternal life.
As we said before, there are seven petitions in the Pater noster. The first three petitions are begun for us in this world, but they will never end in the world to come.
The hallowing of God's glorious name began for us men when Christ became incarnate in our human nature;
but that same hallowing continues forever, because in the eternal life we will always bless and praise God's name.
And God reigns now, and his kingdom stands forever without end, and God's will is done in this life through good people. That same will continues forever into eternity.
The other four petitions belong to this life, and they end with this life.
In this life we need bread, and teaching, and going to the Eucharist.
In the life to come we shall need no earthly food, because then we shall be fed with heavenly food. Here we need teaching and wisdom.
In the heavenly life all those who are now subject to God's commandments through the teaching of wise men will be fully wise and fully learned in spiritual teaching.
And here we need to receive the holy Eucharist for our improvement, but in the heavenly dwelling we will have Christ's body with us, the body in which he reigns forever.
We pray for the forgiveness of our sins in this world, and not in the world to come. The man who will not repent of his sins in his lifetime will get no forgiveness in the world to come.
And in this life we pray that God shield us against the devil's temptations and deliver us from evil.
In the eternal life there will be no temptation and no evil; for no devil and no evil man will come there who could afflict or harm us.
There, soul and body, which now fight against each other in this life, will be in agreement.
There will be no sickness there, no hardship, and no lack of any good thing. Christ will be with us all, and he will do all things for us, without reproach and with all joy.
Christ established this prayer and put it in so few words that all our needs, both spiritual and bodily, are contained in it. And he gave this prayer to all Christian people in common.
He does not say in the prayer, 'My Father, you who are in heaven,' but he says,
"Our Father"; and in the same way all the words that follow after it speak in common of all Christian people.
This shows how much God loves unity and harmony among his people.
According to God's ordinance, all Christian people ought to be as united in peace as if they were one man; therefore woe to the man who breaks that unity.
Just as we have many limbs in one body, and they all obey one head, so we many Christians must obey Christ in unity, because he is our head and we are his limbs.
We can see in our own body how each limb serves the others. The feet carry the whole body, the eyes guide the feet, and the hands prepare the food.
The head would soon lie down if the feet did not carry it, and all the limbs together would soon perish if the hands did not bring food to the mouth.
So too the rich man who sits on his high seat will quickly have to give up his feasting if the servants give up their labours.
Let the rich man be mindful that he must give an account of all the goods that God has lent him, of how he used them.
He who supplies your needs is your hand or your foot. He who teaches you wisdom and brings you onto the right way is your eye.
He who protects you as a father is as if he were your head. The head needs the other limbs just as much as the limbs need the head.
If one limb is sick, all the others suffer along with that one.
So we too, if one of our companions is in some hardship, must all grieve over his trouble and take thought for the remedy, if we are able to remedy it.

And in all things we must keep peace and unity if we wish to have the great honour of being children of God, who is in heaven, where he reigns with all his saints for ever and ever, in eternity. Amen.
